terms.definition: Says what or who something is: name, job, where you're from, the time.
terms.example: Soy Ana, soy de Lima. — I'm Ana, I'm from Lima.
terms.mental_model: ser is the label on the box; estar is a photo of it right now.

terms.definition: Tells where something is or how someone feels right now.
terms.example: Estoy en el bus, ya llego. — I'm on the bus, almost there.
terms.anti_example: Not 'soy cansado' for 'I'm tired': a feeling right now takes estar, so 'estoy cansado'.

terms.definition: Means 'there is' or 'there are'. The same form works for one thing or many.
terms.example: ¿Hay un cajero por aquí? — Is there an ATM around here?
terms.anti_example: Not '¿Dónde hay el baño?' for a place you know exists: ask '¿Dónde está el baño?'

terms.definition: Makes a sentence negative: put 'no' right before the verb.
terms.example: No como carne. — I don't eat meat.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Tengo nada' for 'I have nothing': 'no' stays before the verb, so 'No tengo nada'.

terms.definition: Expresses wanting a thing, or wanting to do something.
terms.example: Quiero un café con leche, por favor.
terms.discussion: 'Quiero…, por favor' is a normal, polite way to order in Latin America. With people, 'te quiero' means 'I love you'.

terms.definition: Lets you say you can do something, or ask if you're allowed to.
terms.example: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? — Can I pay by card?
terms.anti_example: Not '¿Puedes nadar?' for a skill you learned: ask '¿Sabes nadar?' ('saber' = know how).

terms.definition: Thursday, the day between miércoles and viernes.
terms.example: Nos vemos el jueves. — See you Thursday.
terms.anti_example: Not 'en el jueves' for 'on Thursday': Spanish uses just 'el', so 'el jueves'.

terms.definition: Friday, the last workday of the week for most people.
terms.example: ¿Vamos al cine el viernes? — Movies on Friday?
terms.discussion: Written in lowercase, like every weekday: 'el viernes', never 'el Viernes', unless it starts the sentence.

terms.definition: Saturday, the first day of the weekend.
terms.example: El sábado vamos a la playa. — Saturday we're going to the beach.
terms.discussion: Unlike lunes to viernes, it adds -s in the plural: 'los sábados' means every Saturday.

terms.definition: Sunday, the last day of the week on Spanish-language calendars.
terms.example: El domingo no trabajo. — I don't work on Sunday.
terms.discussion: Calendars in Spanish start the week on lunes, so domingo sits in the last column, not the first.
